```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

library(patchwork)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,

)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
```
#`Problem 1`

load the data

```{r}
data("ny_noaa")
```
The NOAA New York weather dataset contains daily meteorological records across multiple weather stations in New York from 1981 to 2010.
The dataset has approximately 2595176 rows (daily observations) and 7 initial columns: `id`, `date`, `prcp`, `snow`, `snwd`, `tmax`, `tmin`.

Missing values are important in this dataset. Many rows contain NA values for temperature and snow/precipitation measurements, meaning some daily records lack valid readings. In `tmax`and `tmin`, over 40 percent of the record is missing which may affect the related plots.

## `1.1`

```{r}
ny_noaa_df = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year  = factor(year(date)),   
    month = month(date),  
    day   = mday(date),
    prcp = prcp / 10,       
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10, 
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  ) 

dim(ny_noaa_df)
summary(ny_noaa_df)

ny_noaa_df |>
  count(snow) |>
  head(10)
```

We split `date` into `year`, `month`, and `day` for future analysis. Among the variables, units of `prcp`, `tmax`, `tmin` need to be divided by 10 because their units are tenth of the reasonable units.

For snow value count, the majority of daily observations have `snow = 0`, meaning no snowfall on those days. We also observe an negative value of snowfall (`snow = -13`) which represents an erroneous data entry and it should be excluded from subsequent analysis.

##`1.2`

```{r}
mean_tmax = ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c(1,7), labels = c("January", "July"))
  ) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) 
```

```{r}
mean_tmax |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, colour = month)) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = month), se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    breaks = seq(1980, 2010, by = 5)
  ) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  labs(
    title = "Average Max Temperature Trend in January and July ", 
    x = "Year", 
    y = "Max Temp",
    caption = "Average Max Temperature in January and in July in Each Station Across Years",
    color = "Month"
  ) 
```

This two-panel figure presents boxplots of average maximum temperature for January and July, grouped by year, with smoothed trend lines overlaid.

July maximum temperatures are consistently much warmer than January maximum temperatures. Temperatures fluctuate from year to year. January shows periodic warmer and colder periods over time, while July temperatures remain relatively stable and warm across decades.

Outliers are present in both months. January has many warm high-value outliers. July also a few low-value outliers, including an unusually cold observation in 1988, representing rare anomalous weather events.

##`1.3`
```{r}
plot_1 = ny_noaa_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) + 
  geom_hex() +
  theme(legend.position = "right") + 
  labs(
    title = "Max Tem vs Min Tem", 
    x = "Minimum temperature", 
    y = "Maximum temperature"
  ) 
  


plot_2 = ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges() +
  scale_y_discrete(
    breaks = seq(1980, 2010, by = 5)
  ) +
  labs(x ="Snowfall (mm)", y =  "Year", title = "Snowfall by year") 

plot_1 + plot_2

```

This two-panel figure contains a hexbin (left) and a ridge plot (right).

The left hexbin plot illustrates the positive correlation between minimum and maximum temperatures, where higher minimums generally align with higher maximums. The color gradient highlights data density, showing that most observations are heavily concentrated in the mild temperature range (min temp between 0°C and 20°C, max temp between 0°C and 30°C), while rare extreme values outliers still exist.

The right ridgeline plot illustrates the probability density distribution of annual snowfall. Across the decades, the snowfall data exhibits a strikingly consistent multimodal distribution, characterized by distinct primary peaks at approximately 10 mm and 20–30 mm, alongside smaller secondary peaks near 50 mm and 75 mm. The temporal stability of these density profiles indicates that the regional snowfall regime is relatively stable over time.
